caption:
Why does the Venus of Willendorf have no face?

She is 11.1 centimetres tall, carved from oolitic limestone and tinted with red ochre, and she was left in the ground around 30,000 years ago. Where a face should be there are circular horizontal bands running right around the head — possibly rows of plaited hair, possibly a headdress. No eyes, no mouth, no nose.

A workman on Josef Szombathy's dig picked her out of the ground near Willendorf, Lower Austria, on 7 August 1908. The record cannot even settle his name: Johann Veran, or Josef Veram.

The stone is not local. Research published in 2022 points to northern Italy near Lake Garda, on the far side of the Alps, as the closest likely source. A weaker candidate is eastern Ukraine, about 1,600 km away — closer to southern Russian sites where similar figurines turn up. Either answer raises the same question about how far Paleolithic people moved.

What she was for is unresolved. "Venus" is a modern label, applied thousands of years after the carving, by archaeologists who assumed a fertility deity; some scholars drop it and say the Woman from Willendorf. Catherine McCoid and LeRoy McDermott proposed the figurines were self-portraits, the body seen foreshortened from above, the missing face explained by the absence of mirrors. Michael Bisson objected that pools and puddles work as mirrors perfectly well.

She probably never had feet and could not stand on her own. She may have been pegged into soft ground.

Images: the figurine in the Naturhistorisches Museum Wien, photographed by Kharmacher, Vassil and Syd Storm; a head detail of a replica; and Hugo Darnaut's 1885 painting of the Willendorf loess cliff.
